tldr: The paper proposes DEPS (Describe, Explain, Plan and Select), an interactive LLM-based planning approach that enables multi-task embodied agents to robustly accomplish 70+ open-world Minecraft tasks by iteratively correcting plan errors and selecting efficient sub-goals based on horizon prediction.
contributions: Identifying two key challenges in open-world task planning: long multi-step reasoning requirements and state-dependent sub-goal feasibility
Proposing DEPS, an interactive planning framework with a descriptor, LLM explainer/planner, and a horizon-predictive goal selector
First zero-shot multi-task agent to robustly accomplish 70+ Minecraft tasks without any demonstration or planning training
Demonstrating general effectiveness on non-open-ended domains (ALFWorld and tabletop manipulation)
methods: The method uses an LLM-based planner to decompose high-level tasks into sub-goal sequences. When execution fails, an event-triggered descriptor summarizes the current state and outcome into structured text feedback. The LLM acts as an explainer to locate errors via self-explanation (e.g., missing required tools), then re-plans with the explanation incorporated. A learned horizon-predictive selector estimates remaining steps to each candidate sub-goal and ranks parallel goals by accessibility, choosing the most efficient path.
results: DEPS is the first zero-shot multi-task agent to robustly accomplish 70+ Minecraft tasks within a limited horizon (3000-12000 steps depending on task difficulty). It nearly doubles the overall success rate compared to language planner baselines using the same initial state and goal-conditioned controller. It also achieves on-par to over 50% relative improvement over existing LLM-based planning methods on ALFWorld and tabletop manipulation environments.
limitations: The approach relies on a single standardized goal-conditioned controller trained by behavior cloning, and performance may vary across different Minecraft versions with differing rules and items. The paper acknowledges that open-world environments pose unique challenges including abundant object types, complex dependencies, and unpredictable transition dynamics that make flawless initial planning extremely difficult.
